body:
# Independent audit: external common-contact dimension drop

Source: `candidate f9c635ce5abe9f17`, including
the explicit active-normal perturbation and deepest-radial-point additions.
**PASS**. The proved conclusion is the sharp bound `gamma_(d-1)` for a
finite whole-space halfspace cover with a common exterior or boundary
contact of one ordinary convex body. No mixed-integer conclusion is
included in this audit.

## 1. Radial convexity, including an origin outside the support

The radial positive intervals are intervals by convexity of the positive
domain of the extended negative power. On the relative interior of every
nontrivial positive radial interval, that finite convex function is
continuous. A normalized ray with positive integral therefore has
strictly increasing C1 quantiles on probability levels strictly between
zero and one, with precisely the derivatives stated in the proof.

For the harmonic radius and weights, the identities are

`a+b=1`, `aR+bS=T`,
`T'=T[a/(R^p f_1)+b/(S^p f_2)]`.

Weighted Hölder with exponents `p+1` and `(p+1)/p` gives exactly

`(a f_1^(-1/(p+1))+b f_2^(-1/(p+1)))^(p+1)
 <=[a/(R^p f_1)+b/(S^p f_2)]T^p`.

Combining this with convexity of the negative power yields the
pointwise lower bound one for the transformed radial probability
integrand. The harmonic radius is strictly increasing, so the
change of variables is valid on every compact probability subinterval;
monotone limits reach the endpoints. If the ray interval begins at
positive radius, the transformed integral is merely over a smaller
interval of the full positive ray, which preserves the inequality.
No unsupported origin-in-body assumption is used.

Positive homogeneity correctly extends the boundary-segment inequality
to contractions and to zero. Bounded support and bounded density give
a uniform finite radial upper bound. For a sequence of nonzero directions
converging to a nonzero direction, one common finite radial interval
dominates the integrands; upper semicontinuity and the dominated upper
limit inequality prove that the radial set is closed. An interior
positive density near zero gives a positive uniform radial lower bound
when that extra hypothesis is invoked. Its convex gauge may take value
infinity outside its positive cone, which is valid when the origin is
outside the original support.

## 2. The negative-power density centerpoint theorem

Joint continuity of cap masses follows from dominated convergence and
the zero Lebesgue measure of every limiting hyperplane. Taking the
minimum over the compact normal sphere preserves continuity. Depth
vanishes on and outside the convex support boundary and is positive
at interior points. Compactness therefore gives an attained maximum
at an interior point.

The active-normal balance argument is rigorous. If a vector v strictly
separates the active normals from zero, there is a common lower bound
for `u dot v` on a neighborhood of them, and a fixed positive cap-mass
gap outside that neighborhood. On a ball centered at the maximizing
point the density has a positive lower bound, by continuity of its
finite negative power. Moving the point by `-epsilon v` increases
every cap in the neighborhood by a uniform positive slab mass. The
source's stated estimate using section radius `R/2` is conservative
and valid when `epsilon|v|<=R/2`; in dimension one its transverse
Hausdorff measure is one. Uniform continuity preserves the other
caps' positive gap. This is an actual depth improvement and proves
zero lies in the convex hull of active normals.

Translating the density to that deepest point preserves the convex
negative-power hypothesis. Applying the radial lemma with `p=r` and
scaling the radial body by `r^(1/r)` makes its volume equal to the
normalized density mass one. Polar integration preserves every cap
mass for halfspaces through zero, with exactly the factor r shown in
the radial formula.

The finitely many balanced active caps cover the entire continuous
space and each has mass alpha in the radial body. Thus every point
has depth at most alpha, while zero has depth exactly alpha by the
through-point mass identities. Zero is a deepest point of that body;
it has not been identified with its centroid. The actual centroid
has classical Grünbaum depth at least `gamma_r`, so alpha is at least
that value. No section-centroid stationarity, equality of coarea
weights, or transfer of ordinary centroids is needed.

## 3. Central projection and its exact exponent

For a strictly exterior contact, the nearest-point separating direction
places all of K between two strictly positive finite t-levels. The
projective map `(t,s)->(t,ts)` has determinant `t^(d-1)`, so the stated
density is exactly the pushforward of uniform d-volume, with total
mass `|K|`.

Its support is compact and convex, and its density is bounded and
upper semicontinuous. To justify positivity at every interior support
point explicitly, take the projection of an interior point of K.
Any other interior projected point lies strictly between that point
and another projected point on the same projected line. The
appropriate positive harmonic reweighting of their original t-levels
lifts this strict projected combination to a combination using an
interior point of K, hence to an interior point of K. Its ray contains
a nontrivial open interval, giving positive projected density.

Applying the radial lemma to `1_K` with `p=d` is legitimate even
though the origin is outside K: its extended negative power is one
on K and infinity elsewhere, a convex function. On the affine plane
`(1,s)`, its radial integral is precisely the projective density.
Restricting the convex gauge therefore gives the exact power
`phi^(-1/d)`, which is the required `-1/(r+1)` for `r=d-1`.

Every original homogeneous cap pulls back to the corresponding
projected affine cap because `t>0`. All-space restrictions immediately
give full volume; empty restrictions can be ignored. The remaining
restricted caps cover the entire projected space, so one contains
the density center and has the claimed `gamma_(d-1)` mass. There is
no replacement of the density by uniform projected volume.

## 4. Boundary passage and sharpness

At a boundary contact, moving the common contact slightly outward in
a supporting direction makes it strictly exterior. Translating every
halfspace by that same vector preserves the whole-space cover. A
finite-index subsequence selects one cap carrying the desired mass
along the exterior approximations. Its indicators converge almost
everywhere on K because the limiting hyperplane has zero d-volume.
Dominated convergence retains the exact constant. No projective
density limit at a boundary anchor is assumed.

For the sharp examples, the cone frustum over a `(d-1)`-simplex with
centroid zero is a full-dimensional compact convex body, and the
barycentric-gradient halfspaces cover the entire ambient space. Every
positive t-section has exactly the simplex centroid-cap fraction
`gamma_(d-1)`, so integration gives equality. Replacing the frustum
by its pyramid gives the boundary-contact equality example. The
halfspaces share a whole contact line; the theorem permits that and
does not require their boundaries to intersect in a single point.

The dimension-one observation uses ordinary halfline containment and
the convention `gamma_0=1`, independently of the radial proof. All
higher-dimensional formulas retain full Lebesgue volume and all
halfspaces are closed.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
